generatedProse.concept-context: Psychology leans heavily on Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle because so much of the discipline is learned by doing: running a study, delivering an intervention, working in a research team. The cycle insists you move past what happened and how it felt to abstract conceptualisation, connecting the experience to theory, evidence or professional guidance, before planning what to change. For a psychologist, that conceptualisation stage is where an anecdote about a group project or a client session becomes genuine professional learning.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students reflect on the same group research project that went badly when an ethics deadline was missed.

Tom stops after the first two stages of the cycle. He describes the missed deadline and the tension it caused, and observes that he felt frustrated and that the team communicated poorly. The account is accurate, but it ends at observation: no concept is brought in to explain it, and no plan follows. It is a description with feelings attached.

Amara carries the same experience through all four stages. After describing and observing, she reaches abstract conceptualisation: drawing on what she knows about group roles and diffusion of responsibility, she sees that no one had owned the ethics submission and that everyone assumed someone else would. Then active experimentation: next time she will propose named roles and a shared timeline at the first meeting. Her plan becomes the start of the next cycle.

Both began from the same project. Only Amara used the whole cycle, turning an event into a concept-led plan rather than a retelling.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, Kolb's cycle turns an experience such as a study or a group project into learning by carrying it through concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation. Used critically, it forces the step from describing what happened to explaining it with concepts and planning what to change. You can now structure a reflection with the cycle, tell critical reflection from description, and reach a reasoned plan. The next lesson turns this into writing.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's reflection critical rather than descriptive?

items.text: She explained the missed deadline using concepts such as group roles and diffusion of responsibility, and reached a concrete plan.
She described the missed deadline and the tension in more vivid detail.
She spent longer describing how frustrated she felt.
She identified which team member was most at fault.

feedback.correct: That's right. Explaining the experience with psychological concepts and reaching a plan is what makes the reflection critical.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the stages of the cycle that Tom left out.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's reflection was critical because she conceptualised the episode with psychological ideas and reached a plan, not because her description was more vivid or her feeling stronger.
